name: PIQA: Physical Interaction Question Answering
description: PIQA is a benchmark dataset for evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding systems. The dataset consists of multiple-choice question answering pairs where a model must choose the most appropriate solution to a physical goal from two options. It contains over 16,000 training QA pairs with approximately 2K development and 3K test examples. The dataset is inspired by instructables.com and focuses on everyday situations with a preference for atypical solutions. Humans achieve 95% accuracy while large pretrained models struggle at around 77%.
creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi
publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI)
citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., and Choi, Y. (2020). PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) annotators who were prompted with links to instructables.com to inspire physical commonsense goal-solution pairs. Annotators were asked to glance at an instructable and construct two component tasks, articulating a physical goal and a valid solution, as well as a 'trick' (an invalid but plausible-sounding alternative solution). Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness. Annotators with low agreement were disqualified. The dataset was further cleaned using the AFLite algorithm to remove annotation artifacts and spurious biases.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. This often meant that correct examples were removed that required expert level knowledge of a domain (e.g., special woodworking terminology) which should not fall under the umbrella of 'commonsense.'
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Instructions and project ideas from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for doing everything from cooking to car repair. Annotators used these as inspiration to construct goal-solution pairs.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The AFLite algorithm was used to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples from the data. AFLite performs systematic data bias reduction by discarding instances whose feature representations are collectively highly indicative of the target label. 5,000 examples from the original dataset were used to fine-tune BERT-Large, and the corresponding embeddings of all remaining instances were computed. AFLite uses an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets of the data to determine whether pre-computed embeddings are strong indicators of the correct answer option.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Data was tokenized using Spacy. Examples were truncated at 150 tokens for model experiments, affecting 1% of the data. The longest 1% of data was removed for certain analyses. AFLite was applied to remove annotation artifacts. Train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were provided with links to instructables.com as inspiration. They were asked to: (1) provide a physical goal, (2) provide a valid solution, and (3) provide a 'trick' - a solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong, often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. A qualification HIT was run prior to the main annotation stage where annotators had to successfully identify (>80%) well-formed vs. underspecified goal-solution pairs. Data was collected in batches and validated by other annotators for correctness. Users with low agreement were disqualified. Annotators were seeded with instructables from six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop. Two examples were drawn per instructable. A diff button was included in the interface to highlight differences between solutions.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed. Human performance was calculated by majority vote. Annotators chosen for human performance evaluation achieved ≥90% on the qualification HIT. Annotator pay averaged >$15/hr according to self-reporting on turkerview.com and timing calculations.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Spacy (for tokenization and POS tagging), BERT-Large (used within AFLite for bias removal), GPT BPE tokenizer (for sequence length analysis)
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance physical commonsense reasoning in AI systems, which is a major challenge on the road to true AI-completeness, including robots that interact with the world and understand natural language. The authors argue that knowledge should be learned from interaction with the world to eventually be communicated with language, and that language-only pretraining is limiting for physical understanding.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset was constructed to be adversarial to BERT. Reporting bias was a challenge during data collection, as annotators tended to gravitate toward prototypical solutions and common tools. AFLite was applied to reduce annotation artifacts and spurious biases. The distribution of referenced objects was flattened by prompting annotators with instructables links. Annotators were seeded with instructables from six categories to encourage diversity.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses on everyday physical commonsense and may not cover expert-level domain knowledge (e.g., special woodworking terminology). Examples requiring expert knowledge were removed during validation. The dataset was constructed to be adversarial to BERT, which may limit its generalizability as a neutral benchmark. Future models trained on large in-domain data may surpass human performance without necessarily achieving true physical understanding.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for benchmarking and evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding models. It can be used for training, validation, and testing of NLP models. It is also designed as a diagnostic tool to probe the physical knowledge of deep pretrained language models. The dataset is not recommended for use cases requiring expert-level domain knowledge.
